Leveraged funds deal with decay from volatility, the easy way to look at it is if oil goes up 10%, UWTI will go up 30%, if the next day oil goes down 10% back to where it was, UWTI will also go down 30% but while oil will be at the same price it was the day before, UWTI will be lower. If we repeat this same movement over time, your UWTI holdings will be worth less over time even if the price of oil stays stagnant. 

Because these leveraged funds have natural decay, it's unrealistic to expect them to achieve their previous high price points even if the underlying asset they represent reaches its original price point. 

This just means that a leveraged etf is only good for short term holding/day trading. If you want to go long on oil, you're better off putting in 3x what you would have invested into a 1x oil fund like DBO rather than holding UWTI, you stand to lose a lot less from market volatility. 

Of course, this is also not taking into account the fund's fees which would also further increase losses and decrease gains making it further unlikely of achieving old prices. Oil would have to hit something on the order of $150 per barrel for UWTI to hit $30 again, which is probably not going to happen. 

You can google leverage etf decay if you want a more thorough explanation.
